translations.title: The Earth's Heart
translations.text:
The Earth's heart
has people who tear at it.
The Earth is very old.
She suffers heart attacks
—in her depths.
Her volcanoes
beat too hard
with too much hatred and lava.

The Earth is in no shape for much exertion;
she is tired.
When children riddled with shrapnel
are buried in her,
she retches.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Poetics
translations.text:
Why, at this point,
should I trouble myself
with writing in magazines, dead pages, or books?
Why should I care about a name
when I already have yours and mine?
Why indifference, conferences,
anthologies, myths?
Why readings, translations,
when everything has already been said?

I have changed
my methods and style.

And now, to work!

To write upon your body
with fingers dipped in wine.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: On the Edge
translations.text:
I am tall;
during the war
I weighed only forty kilos.

I have been on the edge of tuberculosis,
on the edge of prison,
on the edge of friendship,
on the edge of art,
on the edge of suicide,
on the edge of mercy,
on the edge of envy,
on the edge of fame,
on the edge of love,
on the edge of the beach,
and little by little I grew sleepy,
and here I am, sleeping on the edge,
on the edge of waking.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Rooster Alarm Clock
translations.text:
Cock-a-doodle-doo,
here I am,
said the rooster
Hummingbird.

The rooster Hummingbird
had red feathers,
and his suit
was lovely plumage.

Cock-a-doodle-doo.
Get up, farmer,
for the sun
is on its way.

Cock-a-doodle-doo.

Get up, plowman,
wake with joy,
for day is coming.

Cock-a-doodle-doo.

Children of the village,
wake up with a cheer;
they are waiting for you at school.
The village needs no clock:
the rooster alarm clock will do.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: All the Past
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: When a Giant Tree Commits Suicide...
translations.text:
When a giant tree commits suicide,
tired of standing dry and giving no more birds,
without waiting for a man to fell it,
without waiting for the wind,
it releases its last music without leaves
—a symphonic explosion where nests once were—;
all its hollow wood creaks,
two drops of sap still fall
as its trunk bursts through the air;
its tons roll down the mountainside,
wolves weep and deer tremble,
all the squirrels come to meet it,
sensing that something beautiful is dying.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: It Costs a Lot to Be a Poet
translations.text:
It costs a lot, ladies and gentlemen, to be a poet.
People go to bed without a care
—work gives them a good night's sleep.
I work like a slave and come home,
sit at a table without a kitchen,
and begin to ponder what is happening.
Doubt riddles me; everything frightens me.
Shadows begin to devour me;
the hours pass without a yawn;
sleep takes fright and flees from me
—writing keeps me up until dawn.
And then my friends arrange readings for me,
where I turn up and read like a fool,
and people know nothing of this:
that I pour my lifeblood into what I write,
fall from the branch of rhyme,
storm the trenches of anguish;
the ghosts declare me their hero,
and when I finish, I can barely breathe.
It costs a lot, ladies and gentlemen, to be a poet.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: When They Say Your Name
translations.text:
When they say your name,
they steal a little of your name from me;
it seems impossible
that half a dozen letters can say so much.

My madness would be to tear down walls with your name;
I would paint it on every wall;
there would be no well
I would not lean over
to say your name,
no mountain of stone

where I would not shout,
teaching the echo
your six distinct letters.

My madness would be
to teach the birds to sing it,
teach the fish to drink it,
teach people there is nothing
like going mad and repeating your name.

My madness would be to forget everything:
the other twenty-two letters, the numbers,

the books I have read, the verses I have written.
To greet people with your name.
To ask for bread with your name.
“She always says the same thing,” they would say as I passed,
and I would be so proud, so happy, so at ease.

And I will go to the next world with your name on my lips;
to every question I will answer with your name.
The judges and the saints will understand nothing.
God would sentence me to say it forever without stopping.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Autobiography
translations.text:
Gloria Fuertes was born in Madrid
at the age of two days,
for my mother's labor was so difficult
she nearly died giving me life.
At three I could already read,
and at six I could already do my chores.
I was good and thin,
tall and somewhat sickly.
At nine a cart ran into me,
and at fourteen the war caught me;
at fifteen my mother died—she left when I needed her most.
I learned to bargain in the shops
and go to villages for carrots.
Around then I began to fall in love
—I will not name names—;
thanks to that I endured
my youth in the neighborhood.
I wanted to go to war to stop it,
but they stopped me halfway there.
Then I got an office job,
where I work as if I were stupid
—but God and the office boy know I am not.
I write at night
and often go to the countryside.
All my family died years ago,
and I am lonelier than myself.
I have published verses in every calendar,
I write for a children's newspaper,
and I want to buy on installments a real flower
like the ones Pemán sometimes receives.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Unknown Island
translations.text:
I am like that unknown island,
beating as lush trees rock it,
in the middle of a sea
that does not understand me,
surrounded by nothing,
alone, only alone.

On my island are shining birds,
painted by angel painters;
there are beasts that look at me tenderly,
and poisonous flowers.

There are poet streams
and inner voices
of sleeping volcanoes.

Perhaps there is some treasure
deep in my depths.
Who knows whether I have
a diamond in my mountain,
or only a small
piece of coal!

The trees in my island's forest
are you, my verses.
How lovely you sound sometimes
when the great musician, wind,
plays you as the surrounding sea comes in!

If someone reaches this island that I am,
I hope they find something here:
springs of glowing verses
and cascades of peace are what I have.

A name rises through my soul
and will not let me weep my secrets;
and I am happy land, for I have the art
of being happy and poor at once.

It is a pleasure to be unknown,
an unknown island in the eternal ocean.
At the center of the world, without a book,
I know everything, for a messenger came
and left me a cross for life
—and for death, a mystery.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.
